A fall in a store, a parking lot or an apartment stairwell can leave you with injuries, medical bills and time off work you never planned for. In Georgia, the answer depends on what the evidence can prove: whether the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard, how badly you were hurt, your own share of fault and the insurance available to pay. This guide explains those factors rather than quoting averages, because an average says nothing reliable about one person's fall. Roden Law works on a contingency fee: no fees unless we win.

What do you have to prove after a fall in Georgia?
What do you have to prove after a fall in Georgia?

To recover for a fall on a business's property, Georgia courts generally require you to show two things: that the owner knew or should have known about the hazard, and that you did not know about it despite using ordinary care, because of something the owner did or controlled (Robinson v. Kroger Co., 268 Ga. 735 (1997); American Multi-Cinema, Inc. v. Brown, 285 Ga. 442 (2009)).

That test rests on the owner's duty. A business that invites customers onto its property must exercise ordinary care to keep the premises and approaches safe (O.C.G.A. § 51-3-1). Someone on the property for their own purposes, rather than as a customer, is a licensee and can recover only for willful or wanton injury (O.C.G.A. § 51-3-2). A trespasser is owed only the duty not to cause willful or wanton injury (O.C.G.A. § 51-3-3). Those claims are generally much harder to prove.

"Should have known" is where many fall cases are won or lost. Georgia courts generally treat an owner as knowing about a hazard it never actually saw where an employee was nearby and could easily have seen and removed it, or where the hazard was there long enough that a reasonable inspection would have found it.

What if you didn't see the hazard before you fell?
What if you didn't see the hazard before you fell?
You may still have a claim if you didn't see the hazard. Georgia courts generally hold that not looking down at the moment you fell does not, by itself, mean you were careless (Robinson).

Fixed conditions, such as a curb or a step, are treated differently from spills. For a fixed condition you could plainly see, or had safely walked over before, Georgia courts may presume you knew about it. A distraction the owner created or should have anticipated can change that, which is why it matters what drew your attention at the moment you fell.

What damages can you recover after a Georgia slip and fall?
What damages can you recover after a Georgia slip and fall?

Georgia law recognizes economic damages, such as medical expenses, lost wages and lost earning capacity, and noneconomic damages, such as pain, suffering, mental anguish and loss of enjoyment of life (O.C.G.A. § 9-10-184).

For falls on or after April 21, 2025, medical expenses are generally measured by the reasonable value of medically necessary care (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-1.1).

Georgia law sets no formula for pain and suffering. If the case goes to trial, the jury decides what it is worth. That is why treatment records and the accounts of people who see your daily limits carry so much weight.

How does your own fault affect a Georgia slip and fall case?
How does your own fault affect a Georgia slip and fall case?
Your own fault can reduce or end the claim. Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you recover nothing if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33).
Your own fault can reduce or end the claim.
Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you recover nothing if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33).

A separate rule bars recovery if ordinary care would have let you avoid the consequences of the owner's negligence (O.C.G.A. § 51-11-7). In fall cases, owners usually argue that you saw, or should have seen, the hazard, so photos and witness accounts gathered early matter. Who pays for a slip and fall injury in Georgia?
Who pays for a slip and fall injury in Georgia?

The liability insurance of the property owner or the business is usually what pays a Georgia slip and fall claim. More than one party may share responsibility, such as the owner of the property, a tenant business that runs the store and a cleaning or maintenance contractor. Each responsible party pays only its own share of fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), so identifying every one of them early matters.

What if you fell on city, county or State property?
What if you fell on city, county or State property?

A fall on public property carries a written notice deadline that comes due much sooner than the lawsuit deadline. A claim against a Georgia city requires ante litem notice within six months (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5). A claim against a county must be presented within twelve months (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1). Notice of a claim against the State is due within twelve months of when the loss was or should have been discovered (O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26).

How long do you have to file a slip and fall lawsuit in Georgia?
